exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 11–16, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3}\textbf{v}_{3}$$ and $$c_{1} + c_{2} + c_{3} = 1$$ , then $$\textbf{y}$$ is a convex combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}\textbf{,}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ .﻿
(T/F) A set is convex if $$\textbf{x}$$ , $$\textbf{y} \in S$$ implies that the line segment between $$\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ is contained in $$S$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$S$$ is a nonempty set, then $$\text{conv} S$$ contains some points that are not in $$S$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$S$$ and $$T$$ are convex sets, then $$S \cap T$$ is also convex.

(T/F) If $$S$$ is a nonempty subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ and $$\textbf{y} \in$$ $$\text{conv} S$$ , then there exist distinct points $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{6}$$ in $$S$$ such that $$\textbf{y}$$ is a convex combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{6}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$S$$ and $$T$$ are convex sets, then $$S \cup T$$ is also convex.

Let $$S$$ be a convex subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and suppose that $$f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ is a linear transformation. Prove that the set $$f(S) = \{ f(\textbf{x}):\textbf{x} \in S\}$$ is a convex subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .﻿

Let $$f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation and let $$T$$ be a convex subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . Prove that the set $$S = \left\{ \textbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}:f\left( \textbf{x} \right) \in T \right\}$$ is a convex subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .﻿

problem.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ be points in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and define $$\textbf{f}_{0}(t) = (1 - t)\textbf{p}_{0} + t\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{f}_{1}(t) = (1 - t)\textbf{p}_{1} + t\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{g}(t) = ({1 - t})\textbf{f}_{0}(t) + t\textbf{f}_{1}(t)$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . For the points as shown below, draw a picture that shows $$\textbf{f}_{0}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)$$ , $$\textbf{f}_{1}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)$$ , and $$\textbf{g}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)$$ .﻿
Repeat Exercise 25 for $$\textbf{f}_{0}\left( \frac{3}{4} \right)$$ , $$\textbf{f}_{1}\left( \frac{3}{4} \right)$$ , and $$\textbf{g}\left( \frac{3}{4} \right)$$ .﻿

Let $$\textbf{g}(t)$$ be defined as in Exercise 25. Its graph is called a quadratic Bézier curve, and it is used in some computer graphics designs. The points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ are called the control points for the curve. Compute a formula for $$\textbf{g}(t)$$ that involves only $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ . Then show that $$\textbf{g}(t)$$ is in $$\text{conv} \{\textbf{p}_{0},\textbf{p}_{1},\textbf{p}_{2}\}$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ .﻿

Given control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , let $$\textbf{g}_{1}(t)$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ be the quadratic Bézier curve from Exercise 27 determined by $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and let $$\textbf{g}_{2}(t)$$ be defined similarly for $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . For $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ , define $$\textbf{h}(t) = (1 - t)\textbf{g}_{1}(t) + t\textbf{g}_{2}(t)$$ . Show that the graph of $$\textbf{h}(t)$$ lies in the convex hull of the four control points. This curve is called a cubic Bézier curve, and its definition here is one step in an algorithm for constructing Bézier curves (discussed later in Section 8.6). A Bézier curve of degree $$k$$ is determined by $$k + 1$$ control points, and its graph lies in the convex hull of these control points.

problem.paragraph: The points $$v_{1}$$ , $$v_{2}$$ , and $$v_{3}$$ are not orthogonal, so compute $$\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 8 \\ 2 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{p}_{1} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} \mathbf{p}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 0 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
If $$\textbf{p}$$ is a point above $$S$$ , then the line through $$\textbf{p}$$ with slope $$- 1$$ will intersect $$S$$ at two points before it reaches the positive $$x-$$ and $$y \text{-axes}$$ .

list.item: Augment the matrix $$[\begin{matrix} {\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1}} & {\mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1}} \end{matrix}]$$ with both $$\textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , and row reduce: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 8 & - 5 & - 3 \\ - 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & - 3 & - 1 & - 1 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3} & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & - \frac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

The third column shows that $$\textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \frac{1}{3} (\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}) + {\frac{2}{3} }(\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1})$$ , which leads to $$\textbf{p}_{1} = 0\textbf{v}_{1} + \frac{1}{3}\textbf{v}_{2} + \frac{2}{3}\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Thus $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{conv} S$$ . In fact, $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{conv} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . ﻿

The last column of the matrix shows that $$\textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is not a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ . Thus $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is not an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , so $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ cannot possibly be in $$\text{conv} S$$ . ﻿

An alternative method of solution is to row reduce the augmented matrix of homogeneous forms: $$\left[\left(\overset{\sim}{v}\right)_{1} \left(\overset{\sim}{v}\right)_{2} \left(\overset{\sim}{v}\right)_{3} \left(\overset{\sim}{p}\right)_{1} \left(\overset{\sim}{p}\right)_{2}\right] ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
